title: Physics
summary: From measurement to quantum fields. The spine is mechanics; five threshold concepts (Newton's laws, conservation of energy, entropy, relativity of simultaneity, quantum states) change how everything after them is seen.
sources: Halliday, Resnick, Walker: Fundamentals of Physics
Feynman, Leighton, Sands: The Feynman Lectures on Physics
Hestenes, Wells, Swackhamer: Force Concept Inventory (1992)

nodes.label: Measurement & Uncertainty
nodes.summary: Every number in physics carries a unit and an uncertainty; a result without either is not yet a result.
nodes.outcome: Report a measured quantity with unit and propagated uncertainty.
nodes.check: You time 10 swings of a pendulum as 14.2 s ± 0.2 s. What is the period and its uncertainty?
nodes.answer: 1.42 s ± 0.02 s: dividing by an exact count divides the uncertainty too.

nodes.label: Units & Dimensional Analysis
nodes.summary: Equations must balance in dimensions as well as numbers, which lets you guess laws and catch errors before computing.
nodes.outcome: Derive the form of a law (up to a constant) from dimensions alone.
nodes.check: Using dimensions only, how must a pendulum's period depend on its length L and g?
nodes.answer: T ∝ √(L/g): it is the only combination of L [m] and g [m/s²] with units of seconds.

nodes.label: Vectors
nodes.summary: Quantities with direction add head to tail and split into independent components.
nodes.outcome: Resolve a vector into components and add vectors by components.
nodes.check: A 10 N force points 30° above horizontal. What is its horizontal component?

nodes.label: Kinematics
nodes.summary: Position, velocity and acceleration as rates of change of one another; constant-acceleration motion in each axis independently.
nodes.outcome: Predict the trajectory of a projectile from its launch conditions.
nodes.check: A ball is thrown horizontally off a table while another is dropped from the same height. Which lands first?
nodes.answer: They land together: vertical motion is independent of horizontal velocity.

nodes.label: "Motion needs a force"
nodes.summary: The impetus intuition: a moving object must be pushed to keep moving, and stops when the push 'runs out'. The FCI shows it survives a traditional first course.
nodes.outcome: State and refute the impetus model with a frictionless counterexample.
nodes.check: A puck slides across frictionless ice at constant velocity. What net force acts on it?
nodes.answer: Zero. Constant velocity means zero net force; force changes motion, it does not sustain it.

nodes.label: Newton's Laws
nodes.summary: Force causes acceleration, not velocity. Crossing this threshold reorganises every later topic; it is troublesome precisely because everyday experience is full of friction.
nodes.outcome: Draw a free-body diagram and apply ΣF = ma to predict motion.
nodes.check: A book rests on a table. Name the Newton's-third-law partner of the gravitational force of Earth on the book.
nodes.answer: The gravitational force of the book on Earth, not the normal force from the table.

all: on the earth by the book

nodes.label: "Heavier falls faster"
nodes.summary: Aristotle's intuition, contradicted by Galileo: without air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration.
nodes.outcome: Explain why mass cancels in free fall.
nodes.check: In a vacuum, a hammer and a feather are dropped together. Which lands first?
nodes.answer: Together: F = mg and a = F/m = g, so mass cancels (shown on the Moon by Apollo 15).

nodes.label: Forces & Free-Body Diagrams
nodes.summary: Gravity, normal, tension, friction and springs as interactions between pairs of objects, isolated one body at a time.
nodes.outcome: Model a multi-force system and solve for an unknown force.
nodes.check: A 2 kg block hangs from a rope at rest. What is the tension?
nodes.answer: About 19.6 N (T = mg).

nodes.label: "Centrifugal force pushes outward"
nodes.summary: In an inertial frame there is no outward force on a turning object; the net force points inward and the 'outward push' is inertia felt from a rotating frame.
nodes.outcome: Identify the centripetal force in a circular-motion scenario.
nodes.check: A car rounds a flat curve at constant speed. Which force keeps it on the curve?
nodes.answer: Static friction between tyres and road, pointing toward the centre.

nodes.label: Circular Motion
nodes.summary: Changing direction is acceleration: a = v²/r toward the centre, supplied by real forces.
nodes.outcome: Compute the centripetal force needed for a given speed and radius.
nodes.check: If you double the speed on the same curve, by what factor does the needed force change?
nodes.answer: Four times (F ∝ v²).

nodes.label: Conservation of Energy
nodes.summary: A single number that stays fixed through every transformation. It replaces step-by-step force accounting with before-and-after bookkeeping.
nodes.outcome: Solve a motion problem with energy conservation where forces would be awkward.
nodes.check: A ball is released from rest 5 m up a frictionless ramp. What is its speed at the bottom?
nodes.answer: √(2gh) ≈ 9.9 m/s, regardless of the ramp's shape.

nodes.label: Work & Power
nodes.summary: Work is force along displacement; power is the rate of doing work.
nodes.outcome: Compute work done by a variable force as an area under F(x).
nodes.check: You carry a box horizontally at constant velocity. How much work does gravity do on it?
nodes.answer: Zero: gravity is perpendicular to the displacement.

nodes.label: Momentum & Collisions
nodes.summary: Total momentum is conserved whenever external forces vanish, in every collision, elastic or not.
nodes.outcome: Predict final velocities in a 1D collision.
nodes.check: A 1 kg cart at 2 m/s sticks to an identical cart at rest. Final speed?
nodes.answer: 1 m/s (momentum 2 kg·m/s shared by 2 kg).

nodes.label: Rotational Dynamics
nodes.summary: Torque, moment of inertia and angular momentum: Newton's laws for spinning bodies.
nodes.outcome: Use τ = Iα and conservation of angular momentum.
nodes.check: A skater pulls in their arms. What happens to the spin rate, and why?
nodes.answer: It increases: I decreases and L = Iω is conserved.

nodes.label: Universal Gravitation
nodes.summary: The same inverse-square force drops apples and holds orbits.
nodes.outcome: Derive orbital speed from F = GMm/r².
nodes.check: Why do astronauts on the ISS float, if gravity there is ~90% of surface gravity?
nodes.answer: They are in free fall together with the station; floating is falling around the Earth.

nodes.label: Simple Harmonic Motion
nodes.summary: Any restoring force proportional to displacement gives sinusoidal motion with a period independent of amplitude.
nodes.outcome: Predict the period of a spring or small-angle pendulum.
nodes.check: Does a pendulum's period change if you double its mass?
nodes.answer: No: T = 2π√(L/g), independent of mass (for small angles).

nodes.label: Waves & Superposition
nodes.summary: Disturbances that carry energy, not matter; overlapping waves add, producing interference and standing waves.
nodes.outcome: Predict interference maxima from path difference.
nodes.check: Two speakers emit the same tone. You stand where the path difference is half a wavelength. What do you hear?
nodes.answer: Near-silence: destructive interference.

nodes.label: Temperature & Heat
nodes.summary: Temperature measures average microscopic kinetic energy; heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference.
nodes.outcome: Apply the first law of thermodynamics to a gas process.
nodes.check: Metal and wood in the same room feel different temperatures. Are they?
nodes.answer: No, same temperature; metal conducts heat away from your hand faster.

nodes.label: "Heat and temperature are the same"
nodes.summary: Conflating a state variable (temperature) with an energy transfer (heat).
nodes.outcome: Distinguish heat from temperature with a phase-change example.
nodes.check: Ice melts in a glass at 0 °C while absorbing heat. What happens to its temperature?
nodes.answer: It stays at 0 °C: the heat breaks bonds rather than raising temperature.

nodes.label: Entropy & the Second Law
nodes.summary: Isolated systems drift toward more probable macrostates. This is where the arrow of time enters physics.
nodes.outcome: Explain irreversibility in terms of counting microstates.
nodes.check: Why does a dropped egg never unscramble, though no law of mechanics forbids it?
nodes.answer: The unscrambled macrostate has overwhelmingly fewer microstates; it is possible but absurdly improbable.

nodes.label: Statistical Mechanics
nodes.summary: Thermodynamics derived from the statistics of very many particles: the Boltzmann factor e^(−E/kT).
nodes.outcome: Use the Boltzmann factor to compare occupation of two energy levels.
nodes.check: As temperature rises, what happens to the ratio of high- to low-energy particles?
nodes.answer: It increases toward 1: e^(−ΔE/kT) grows as T grows.

nodes.label: Electric Charge & Fields
nodes.summary: Charges create fields; fields push charges. Coulomb's law and Gauss's law.
nodes.outcome: Compute the field of a point charge and a charged plane.
nodes.check: What is the electric field inside a charged, conducting hollow sphere?
nodes.answer: Zero (Gauss's law; charge sits on the surface).

nodes.label: "Current gets used up"
nodes.summary: The belief that bulbs consume current, so less flows back to the battery. Current is conserved; energy is what gets transferred.
nodes.outcome: Explain series circuits with charge conservation.
nodes.check: Two bulbs in series: is the current after the second bulb less than before the first?
nodes.answer: No, it is the same everywhere in a series loop; energy, not charge, is used.

nodes.label: Circuits
nodes.summary: Potential difference drives current through resistance; Kirchhoff's rules are charge and energy conservation.
nodes.outcome: Analyse a two-loop circuit with Kirchhoff's rules.
nodes.check: Adding a second identical bulb in parallel: does the battery's current rise or fall?
nodes.answer: It doubles: total resistance halves.

nodes.label: Magnetism & Induction
nodes.summary: Moving charges make magnetic fields; changing magnetic flux makes electric fields (Faraday).
nodes.outcome: Predict induced current direction with Lenz's law.
nodes.check: A magnet falls through a copper tube. Why does it fall slowly?
nodes.answer: Induced eddy currents create a field opposing its motion (Lenz's law).

nodes.label: Maxwell's Equations
nodes.summary: Four equations unify electricity, magnetism and light.
nodes.outcome: Show that Maxwell's equations predict waves travelling at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).
nodes.check: What does Maxwell's displacement current fix in Ampère's law?
nodes.answer: It makes the law consistent for changing fields (e.g. a charging capacitor) and permits EM waves.

nodes.label: Light & Optics
nodes.summary: Light as an EM wave: reflection, refraction, diffraction, and the thin-lens equation.
nodes.outcome: Locate an image with the thin-lens equation.
nodes.check: Why does a straw look bent in a glass of water?
nodes.answer: Refraction: light changes direction crossing the water–air boundary.

nodes.label: Special Relativity
nodes.summary: The speed of light is the same for all observers, so simultaneity, time and length are frame-dependent.
nodes.outcome: Compute time dilation for a moving clock.
nodes.check: A muon lives 2.2 µs at rest but reaches the ground from 15 km up. How?
nodes.answer: In Earth's frame its clock runs slow (time dilation); in its frame the atmosphere is length-contracted.

nodes.label: Lagrangian Mechanics
nodes.summary: Mechanics from one scalar, L = T − V, and the principle of stationary action.
nodes.outcome: Derive equations of motion from a Lagrangian.
nodes.check: What is the advantage of generalized coordinates for a bead on a rotating hoop?
nodes.answer: Constraint forces drop out; one coordinate (the angle) describes the motion.

nodes.label: "Electrons orbit like planets"
nodes.summary: The Bohr picture taken literally. Electrons are described by probability amplitudes, not trajectories.
nodes.outcome: Contrast an orbital with an orbit.
nodes.check: Where is the electron in a hydrogen 1s state?
nodes.answer: It has no definite position; the 1s orbital gives the probability density of finding it.

nodes.label: Quantum Mechanics
nodes.summary: States are vectors, measurements are probabilistic, and observables need not commute.
nodes.outcome: Compute measurement probabilities from a state vector.
nodes.check: A qubit is (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2. What is the probability of measuring 1?
nodes.answer: 1/2 (the squared magnitude of the amplitude).
